statement: Water flows through a pipe with an inside diameter of 2 cm at a speed of 50 cm per second, filling the pipe completely. How many litres of water come out of the pipe each minute? (1 litre is $1000 \text{ cm}^3$.)

choices.misconception: I used the diameter, 2 cm, as the radius when I found the area of the pipe's cross-section.
I found the volume per second, $50\pi \text{ cm}^3 = 0.05\pi$ litres, and forgot to multiply by 60 for a minute.
I found $3000\pi \text{ cm}^3$ per minute and forgot to convert cubic centimetres to litres.
I thought a litre was $100 \text{ cm}^3$ when converting from cubic centimetres.

hints: Picture the column of water that leaves in one second.
Each second a cylinder of water as long as the distance flowed comes out. Find its volume, scale to a minute, and convert units only at the end. Check radius versus diameter.
The cross-section is $\pi \times 1^2 = \pi \text{ cm}^2$. Each second $50\pi \text{ cm}^3$ comes out, so each minute $3000\pi \text{ cm}^3$.

solutions.reliable: The radius is 1 cm, so the cross-section has area $\pi \times 1^2 = \pi \text{ cm}^2$. In one second the water moves 50 cm, so a cylinder of volume $50\pi \text{ cm}^3$ leaves the pipe. In one minute that is $60 \times 50\pi = 3000\pi \text{ cm}^3$, which is $3\pi$ litres, about 9.4 litres. The transferable idea: carry the units through every step and re-read what unit the question wants before answering.

whyOnTest: Three unit traps sit in one short flow calculation: radius versus diameter, seconds versus minutes, and cubic centimetres versus litres.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
